newsitem.title: CHINA: China calls for new large and small coal mines.
newsitem.headline: China calls for new large and small coal mines.

text.p: China should put equal emphasis on building small local coal mines and large state-owned pits as the nation struggles to power its booming economy, state media on Thursday quoted Premier Li Peng as saying.

China would continue to rely on coal for more than 70 percent of its energy far into the future, although Beijing was pushing nuclear and hydropower projects, Li wrote in an article issued by the official Xinhua news agency.
The national coal industry would grow at a rate of 2.3 percent a year until 2000, when output would reach 1.45 billion tonnes and exports would be 50 million tonnes, Li said.
China produced 1.38 billion tonnes of raw coal last year, of which mines at the township level accounted for around 610 million tonnes, he said.
"China's coal industry should place equal emphasis on the construction of both the large state mines and the smaller local ones," Xinhua quoted him as saying.

Local mines tapped China's plentiful rural labour to exploit piecemeal coal resources. They often relied on investments by farmers themselves, easing demands for state funds and providing an escape route from poverty for rural dwellers, he said.
However, action was needed to cut pollution and boost safety at inefficient and poorly managed local mines, where accidents kill thousands of miners every year, he said.
Large and medium-sized state-owned mines remained the driving force of China's coal industry, with key state mines last year accounting for 530 million tonnes of output, he said.

China had installed electricity generation capacity of 230,000 megawatts, but per-capita energy consumption was still equivalent to only 1.14 tonnes of standard coal -- below the global average, he said.
Beijing would work to stabilise oil and gas production in its oldest fields in eastern China while developing newfound reserves in the northwest, Li said.

In 1996, combined oil output for eastern fields including Daqing, Shengli, and Liaohe reached more than 120 million tonnes, with western fields pumping 20 million tonnes and offshore fields accounting for more than 15 million tonnes.
Total natural gas output was 20.1 billion cubic metres.
Further growth was needed to fuel China's booming economy, although the shift toward intensive development meant energy output could lag economic growth slightly, the premier said.
The ratio of the increase of electricity output to growth of gross domestic product (GDP) was expected to be around 0.8.
Hydropower should eventually account for about 30 percent of China's electricity demand and small hydroelectric power plants should be extended in rural areas, he said.
More rational electricity billing was needed under which the cost of power would vary by industry and location, he said.

Between 2001 and 2005, China planned four nuclear power projects with eight generating units and a total installed capacity of 6,600 megawatts, or about two percent of the future national total, he said.
China's current three nuclear generating units, had an installed capacity of 2,100 megawatts, he said.
